claim: ZMYM2 is a zinc finger transcriptional regulator that plays a key role in promoting and maintaining cell identity.
source: ZMYM2 is a zinc finger transcriptional regulator that plays a key role in promoting and maintaining cell identity.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a general characterization of ZMYM2 function, supported by the broader literature context.

claim: ZMYM2 has been implicated in congenital anomalies of the kidney where its activity is diminished.
source: It has been implicated in several diseases such as congenital anomalies of the kidney where its activity is diminished and cancer where it participates in oncogenic fusion protein events.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and referenced in the introduction with citation to Connaughton et al., 2020.

claim: ZMYM2 participates in oncogenic fusion protein events in cancer.
source: It has been implicated in several diseases such as congenital anomalies of the kidney where its activity is diminished and cancer where it participates in oncogenic fusion protein events.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by citations in the introduction (Xiao et al., 1998; Reiter et al., 1998).

claim: ZMYM2 is part of distinct chromatin-bound complexes including the LSD1-CoREST-HDAC1 corepressor complex.
source: Here we studied ZMYM2 function in human cells and demonstrate that ZMYM2 is part of distinct chromatin-bound complexes including the established LSD1-CoREST-HDAC1 corepressor complex.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RIME mass spectrometry data and previous literature (Gocke and Yu, 2008).

claim: ZMYM2 has functional and physical interactions with ADNP.
source: We also identify new functional and physical interactions with ADNP and TRIM28/KAP1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RIME data (Figure 1A), co-IP experiments (Figure 1C), and ChIP-seq overlap (Figure 1E).

claim: ZMYM2 has functional and physical interactions with TRIM28/KAP1.
source: We also identify new functional and physical interactions with ADNP and TRIM28/KAP1.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RIME data (Figure 1A), co-IP experiments (Figure 4A), and ChIP-seq overlap (Figure 2A).

claim: The ZMYM2-TRIM28 complex forms in a SUMO-dependent manner.
source: The ZMYM2-TRIM28 complex forms in a SUMO-dependent manner and is associated with repressive chromatin.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by co-IP experiments showing binding only in the presence of NEM (Figure 4A).

claim: The ZMYM2-TRIM28 complex is associated with repressive chromatin.
source: The ZMYM2-TRIM28 complex forms in a SUMO-dependent manner and is associated with repressive chromatin.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ChIP-seq data showing enrichment of H3K9me3 and depletion of active chromatin marks at cluster 1 regions (Figure 2A, B).

claim: ZMYM2 and TRIM28 show strong functional similarity and co-regulate a large number of genes.
source: ZMYM2 and TRIM28 show strong functional similarity and co-regulate a large number of genes.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by RNA-seq data showing significant overlap in genes regulated by both factors (Figure 4C).

claim: There are no strong links between ZMYM2-TRIM28 binding events and nearby individual gene regulation.
source: However, there are no strong links between ZMYM2-TRIM28 binding events and nearby individual gene regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by analysis showing few differentially expressed genes near ZMYM2 peaks (Figure 5A, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).

claim: ZMYM2-TRIM28 appears to regulate genes in a more regionally defined manner within TADs.
source: Instead, ZMYM2-TRIM28 appears to regulate genes in a more regionally defined manner within TADs where it can directly regulate co-associated retrotransposon expression.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by TAD analysis showing enrichment of upregulated genes in TADs containing cluster 1 peaks (Figure 5C).

claim: ZMYM2-TRIM28 can directly regulate co-associated retrotransposon expression.
source: Instead, ZMYM2-TRIM28 appears to regulate genes in a more regionally defined manner within TADs where it can directly regulate co-associated retrotransposon expression.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by data showing ZMYM2 binding to LTR elements and their upregulation upon ZMYM2 depletion (Figure 6A, D).

claim: Different types of ZMYM2 binding complex associate with and regulate distinct subclasses of retrotransposons.
source: We find that different types of ZMYM2 binding complex associate with and regulate distinct subclasses of retrotransposons, with ZMYM2-ADNP complexes at SINEs and ZMYM2-TRIM28 complexes at LTR elements.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ChIP-seq data showing cluster 2 enriched for SINEs and cluster 1 enriched for LTRs (Figure 6A).

claim: ZMYM2-ADNP complexes associate with SINEs.
source: We find that different types of ZMYM2 binding complex associate with and regulate distinct subclasses of retrotransposons, with ZMYM2-ADNP complexes at SINEs and ZMYM2-TRIM28 complexes at LTR elements.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ChIP-seq data showing ADNP enrichment in cluster 2 which is enriched for SINEs (Figure 3B, C and Figure 6A).

claim: ZMYM2-TRIM28 complexes associate with LTR elements.
source: We find that different types of ZMYM2 binding complex associate with and regulate distinct subclasses of retrotransposons, with ZMYM2-ADNP complexes at SINEs and ZMYM2-TRIM28 complexes at LTR elements.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by ChIP-seq data showing TRIM28 enrichment in cluster 1 which is enriched for LTRs (Figure 2A and Figure 6A).

claim: ZMYM2 was originally identified as part of an oncogenic fusion protein with FGFR1 in myeloproliferative disease.
source: The zinc finger protein ZMYM2 (otherwise known as ZNF198) was originally identified as part of an oncogenic fusion protein with the receptor tyrosine kinase FGFR1 in myeloproliferative disease (Xiao et al., 1998; Reiter et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to original studies.

claim: The N-terminal portion of ZMYM2 promotes the oligomerisation and activation of FGFR1.
source: In this context, the N-terminal portion of ZMYM2 promotes the oligomerisation and activation of FGFR1 (Xiao et al., 2000).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Xiao et al., 2000.

claim: Heterozygous loss of function ZMYM2 mutations lead to congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT) and chronic kidney disease.
source: Further disease links have recently been uncovered where heterozygous loss of function ZMYM2 mutations lead to congenital anomalies of the kidney and urinary tract (CAKUT) and chronic kidney disease (Connaughton et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Connaughton et al., 2020.

claim: ZMYM2 plays important roles in the early stages of embryonic stem cell (ESC) differentiation and commitment.
source: The latter observation suggests a potential developmental role and ZMYM2 has been shown to play important roles in the early stages of embryonic stem cell (ESC) differentiation and commitment.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction and supported by citations to Yang et al., 2020 and Lezmi et al., 2020.

claim: ZMYM2 promotes the transition from totipotency to pluripotency in mice.
source: ZMYM2 promotes the transition from totipotency to pluripotency in mice (Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Yang et al., 2020.

claim: ZMYM2 plays a key role in determining ESC identity by allowing the transition to and maintenance of the primed pluripotent state in human cells.
source: Similarly, in human cells, ZMYM2 plays a key role in determining ESC identity by allowing the transition to and maintenance of the primed pluripotent state (Lezmi et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Lezmi et al., 2020.

claim: ZMYM2 plays a key role in opposing reprogramming in human fibroblasts where ZMYM2 loss increases reprogramming efficiency.
source: Furthermore, ZMYM2 has been shown to play a key role in opposing reprogramming in human fibroblasts where ZMYM2 loss increases reprogramming efficiency (Toh et al., 2016; Lawrence et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Toh et al., 2016 and Lawrence et al., 2019.

claim: ZMYM2 has been shown to act as a transcriptional repressor.
source: Molecularly, ZMYM2 has been shown to act as a transcriptional repressor and can bind to the LSD1-CoREST-HDAC1 corepressor complex (LCH) via its zinc fingers (Gocke and Yu, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Gocke and Yu, 2008.

claim: ZMYM2 can bind to the LSD1-CoREST-HDAC1 corepressor complex (LCH) via its zinc fingers.
source: Molecularly, ZMYM2 has been shown to act as a transcriptional repressor and can bind to the LSD1-CoREST-HDAC1 corepressor complex (LCH) via its zinc fingers (Gocke and Yu, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Gocke and Yu, 2008.

claim: ZMYM2 promotes pluripotency in mice through the LSD1-CoREST-HDAC1 repressive complex.
source: It is through this repressive complex that ZMYM2 promotes pluripotency in mice (Yang et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Yang et al., 2020.

claim: ZMYM2 has been shown to have an interaction with the transcription factor TBX18 with a potential role in ureter development.
source: However, ZMYM2 has been shown to have an increasingly complex set of interaction partners such as the transcription factors TBX18 with a potential role in ureter development (Lüdtke et al., 2022) and B-MYB and hence a potential link to cell cycle control (Cibis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Lüdtke et al., 2022.

claim: ZMYM2 has been shown to have an interaction with B-MYB and hence a potential link to cell cycle control.
source: However, ZMYM2 has been shown to have an increasingly complex set of interaction partners such as the transcription factors TBX18 with a potential role in ureter development (Lüdtke et al., 2022) and B-MYB and hence a potential link to cell cycle control (Cibis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Cibis et al., 2020.

claim: ZMYM2 was detected as a component of repressive complexes in proteomic screens using LSD1/KDM1A and HDAC2 as baits.
source: Proteomic screens have also revealed multiple ZMYM2 binding partners, either from using ZMYM2 itself as a bait (Connaughton et al., 2020) or through detection as a component of other repressive complexes by using baits such as LSD1/KDM1A and HDAC2 (Hakimi et al., 2003; Shi et al., 2005).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citations to Hakimi et al., 2003 and Shi et al., 2005.

claim: ZMYM2 can antagonise 53BP1 function at DNA double strand breaks to favour repair by homologous recombination.
source: The range of interaction partners solidifies ZMYM2 as a potential transcriptional repressor protein, but additional roles are hinted at such as DNA repair, exemplified by its ability to antagonise 53BP1 function at DNA double strand breaks to favour repair by homologous recombination (Lee et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Lee et al., 2022.

claim: ZMYM2 was identified in a screen for multi-SUMO binding proteins.
source: We identified ZMYM2 in a screen for multi-SUMO binding proteins (Aguilar-Martinez et al., 2015) which builds on the complex interplay previously observed between ZMYM2 and SUMO.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Aguilar-Martinez et al., 2015.

claim: ZMYM2 has non-covalent SUMO binding activity.
source: Additional work supports the non-covalent SUMO binding activity of ZMYM2 (Guzzo et al., 2014) although the two studies differed in mapping of the SUMO interacting motifs, with the former mapping them to the N-terminal part of the protein and the latter mapping them to the centrally located zinc finger region.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Guzzo et al., 2014.

claim: ZMYM2 itself is covalently modified with SUMO.
source: Furthermore, ZMYM2 itself is covalently modified with SUMO (Kunapuli et al., 2006) suggesting a complex and important role for SUMO in determining ZMYM2 activity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Kunapuli et al., 2006.

claim: SUMO binding is needed for recruitment of ZMYM2 to chromatin.
source: Indeed, SUMO binding is needed for recruitment of ZMYM2 to chromatin (Aguilar-Martinez et al., 2015) and the ability of ZMYM2 to recruit SUMOylated HDAC-1 (Gocke and Yu, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Aguilar-Martinez et al., 2015.

claim: ZMYM2 has the ability to recruit SUMOylated HDAC-1.
source: Indeed, SUMO binding is needed for recruitment of ZMYM2 to chromatin (Aguilar-Martinez et al., 2015) and the ability of ZMYM2 to recruit SUMOylated HDAC-1 (Gocke and Yu, 2008).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with citation to Gocke and Yu, 2008.

claim: TRIM28 and ADNP are the highest scoring interactors with ZMYM2 in RIME experiments.
source: Among these, the highest scoring interactors were the transcriptional co-regulators TRIM28 and ADNP (Figure 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1A with spectral count data from RIME experiments.

claim: ZMYM2 and ADNP are part of a larger interacting network of proteins including CHD4 and CBX1/HP1β.
source: ZMYM2 and ADNP are part of a larger interacting network of proteins identified in the RIME analysis (Figure 1B), which includes the other two components of the ChAHP complex, CHD4 and CBX1/HP1β (Kaaij et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 1B showing the protein interaction network.

claim: The GTF3C complex was identified as a prominent complex in ZMYM2 RIME experiments.
source: Another prominent complex identified was the GTF3C complex (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A) which is consistent with a previous study that identified ZMYM2 from reciprocal RIME experiment using GTF3C2 as bait (Ferrari et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results with reference to Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and citation to Ferrari et al., 2020.

claim: A large proportion of ZMYM2 interactors were previously identified in proteomic screens from mouse ESCs and human HEK293 cells.
source: A large proportion of the interactors were previously identified in two proteomic screens for ZMYM2 binding proteins from mouse ESCs (Yang et al., 2020) and/or human HEK293 cells (Connaughton et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to Yang et al., 2020 and Connaughton et al., 2020.

claim: 10 ZMYM2 binding proteins were uniquely identified in this study, including SUMO2 and SUMO3.
source: However, 10 ZMYM2 binding proteins were uniquely identified here, including SUMO2 and SUMO3.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on comparison with previous studies.

claim: Endogenous ZMYM2 and ADNP interact as validated by co-immunoprecipitation analysis.
source: We validated interactions between endogenous ZMYM2 and ADNP by co-immunoprecipitation analysis (Figure 1C) and also confirmed interactions of ADNP with the closely related ZMYM3 paralogue (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1C.

claim: ADNP interacts with the ZMYM3 paralogue.
source: We validated interactions between endogenous ZMYM2 and ADNP by co-immunoprecipitation analysis (Figure 1C) and also confirmed interactions of ADNP with the closely related ZMYM3 paralogue (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ZMYM2 and ZMYM3 were detected in mass spectrometry datasets along with ADNP.
source: This data is consistent with the identification of ZMYM2 and ZMYM3 in other mass spectrometry datasets along with ADNP (Ostapcuk et al., 2018; Connaughton et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citations to Ostapcuk et al., 2018 and Connaughton et al., 2020.

claim: ADNP2 was detected as a ZMYM2 interactor.
source: We also detected the ADNP paralogue ADNP2 as a ZMYM2 interactor.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on RIME data.

claim: 5108 ADNP peaks were found in both ChIP-seq datasets in U2OS cells.
source: First, we performed two independent ChIP-seq experiments for ADNP in U2OS cells and uncovered 5108 peaks found in both datasets.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on ChIP-seq analysis.

claim: ADNP peaks showed enrichment of binding motifs for HBP1 and IRF, both found in over 35% of target regions.
source: These ADNP peaks showed enrichment of binding motifs for several transcription factors with the top two motifs for HBP1 and IRF both found in over 35% of target regions (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1D with motif analysis data.

claim: The top scoring motif for ADNP previously identified from ChIP-seq in mouse embryonic stem cells was found in 15% of ADNP peaks in U2OS cells.
source: The top scoring motif for ADNP previously identified from ChIP-seq in mouse embryonic stem cells CGCCCYCTNSTG (Ostapcuk et al., 2018), was not identified in this unbiased analysis. We therefore searched for the motif in the ADNP peaks and found 775 in 5108 peaks (15%) which was a substantially higher frequency than in a background dataset (9.5%) but well below the 63% frequency found in mouse embryonic stem cells.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on motif analysis with citation to Ostapcuk et al., 2018.

claim: There is a significant overlap in chromatin occupancy of ZMYM2 with ADNP peaks.
source: Co-binding on chromatin with ZMYM2 is inferred as there is a significant overlap in chromatin occupancy of ZMYM2 with the ADNP peaks (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1E as a Venn diagram.

claim: Depletion of either ADNP or ZMYM2 gave roughly equivalent numbers of up and downregulated genes.
source: Depletion of either factor alone gave roughly equivalent numbers of up and downregulated genes (Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on RNA-seq analysis.

claim: There is a highly significant overlap in the genes upregulated following depletion of either ADNP or ZMYM2.
source: However, there was a highly significant overlap in the genes upregulated following depletion of either factor, and also a highly significant overlap in the genes downregulated following reductions in either protein (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1G with p-values.

claim: There is a highly significant overlap in the genes downregulated following depletion of either ADNP or ZMYM2.
source: However, there was a highly significant overlap in the genes upregulated following depletion of either factor, and also a highly significant overlap in the genes downregulated following reductions in either protein (Figure 1G).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1G with p-values.

claim: Gene regulation showing reciprocal directionality following either ADNP or ZMYM2 depletion showed a very small and insignificant overlap.
source: Conversely, in contrast to these similarities, gene regulation showing reciprocal directionality following either ADNP or ZMYM2 depletion showed a very small and insignificant overlap (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C) and this is further emphasised by a scatter plot depicting this data (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and 1E.

claim: ZMYM2 and ADNP co-ordinately control gene activity through a transcriptional regulatory complex.
source: Together these results demonstrate that ZMYM2 can function through a transcriptional regulatory complex containing ADNP to co-ordinately control gene activity.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the combined physical and functional interaction data.

claim: Three distinct clusters of ZMYM2 binding regions were revealed by clustering analysis.
source: We took a ZMYM2-centric view of the data and plotted the signal for the other chromatin binding/modification events centred on the ZMYM2 binding peaks and then clustered the data (Figure 2A and B). Three distinct clusters were revealed.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Cluster 3 exhibits ZMYM2 binding but little evidence of any other binding/modification events.
source: Cluster 3 exhibits ZMYM2 binding but little evidence of any other binding/modification events.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the clustering analysis shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Cluster 1 is enriched for both wild-type ZMYM2 and TRIM28 binding.
source: However, cluster 1 is enriched for both wild-type ZMYM2 and TRIM28 binding.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on the clustering analysis shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Cluster 1 is relatively depleted of ATAC-seq and H3K18ac signal, suggesting that regions occupied by both ZMYM2 and TRIM28 are not areas of active chromatin.
source: This cluster is relatively depleted of ATAC-seq and H3K18ac signal, suggesting that regions occupied by both ZMYM2 and TRIM28 are not areas of active chromatin (Figure 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Stronger levels of H3K9me3 were observed in cluster 1 in H1 ESCs.
source: Indeed, when we mapped H3K9me3 signal for H1 ESCs to the ZMYM2 binding regions, stronger levels of this repressive mark were observed in cluster 1 despite the differing cell types (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: H3K9me3 occupancy at ZMYM2 binding sites from cluster 1 was validated in U2OS cells.
source: We validated H3K9me3 occupancy at ZMYM2 binding sites from cluster 1 in U2OS cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1B with ChIP-qPCR data.

claim: SUMO2/3 is strongly detected in cluster 1.
source: SUMO2/3 is also strongly detected in cluster 1 and SUMO has often been associated with transcriptional repressive activity (reviewed in Garcia-Dominguez and Reyes, 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: A cluster of ZMYM2 binding regions in mouse ESCs was strongly associated with TRIM28, SUMO and H3K9me3.
source: We also interrogated ChIP-seq data from mouse ESCs and found that a cluster of ZMYM2 binding regions (cluster B) was strongly associated with TRIM28, SUMO and H3K9me3, further validating our results from human U2OS cells (Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1C and D.

claim: ZMYM2 cluster 2 shows little TRIM28 binding and higher levels of ATAC-seq and H3K18ac signal, suggestive of more active chromatin.
source: In contrast, ZMYM2 cluster 2 shows little TRIM28 binding and higher levels of ATAC-seq and H3K18ac signal (Figure 2A and B; Figure 2—figure supplement 1E), suggestive of more active chromatin.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 2A, B and Figure 2—figure supplement 1E.

claim: Binding of the SUMO binding defective ZMYM2(SIM2mut) is strong in cluster 2 and SUMO occupancy is weaker suggesting that ZMYM2 activity at this cluster is independent of its SUMO binding activity.
source: Conversely, binding of the SUMO binding defective ZMYM2(SIM2mut) is strong and SUMO occupancy is weaker suggesting that ZMYM2 activity at this cluster is independent of its SUMO binding activity.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on ChIP-seq data shown in Figure 2A and B.

claim: Numerous significantly enriched motifs were found in clusters 1 and 2 which differed between clusters.
source: Next we searched for over-represented binding motifs in each ZMYM2 cluster and found numerous significantly enriched motifs which differed between clusters 1 and 2 (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3A.

claim: Several of the motifs in cluster 2 are the same as in the peaks bound by ADNP, including motifs for HBP1 and CTCFL/BORIS.
source: Interestingly, several of the motifs in cluster 2 are the same as in the peaks bound by ADNP (Figure 1D), including motifs for HBP1 and CTCFL/BORIS.
evidence: This is stated in the results comparing Figure 3A and Figure 1D.

claim: The HBP1 motif was previously observed as a preferred binding motif for the paralogue ZMYM3.
source: The HBP1 motif was also previously observed as a preferred binding motif for the paralogue ZMYM3 (Partridge et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to Partridge et al., 2020.

claim: Highest ADNP occupancy was found in cluster 2 as predicted from the motif analysis.
source: Given the similarity in binding motifs, we superimposed the ADNP ChIP-seq signal onto the ZMYM2 clusters and found highest ADNP occupancy in cluster 2 as predicted from the motif analysis (Figure 3B and C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3B and C.

claim: Cluster 3 ZMYM2 peaks showed enrichment of ASCL2 and ETS transcription factor binding motifs.
source: Cluster 3 ZMYM2 peaks showed enrichment of a different set of DNA binding motifs with ASCL2 and ETS transcription factor binding motifs figuring prominently (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Cluster 1 peaks showed a predominantly intergenic or intronic distribution.
source: Differences were also observed in genomic location distributions of each cluster with cluster 1 peaks showing a predominantly intergenic or intronic distribution, whereas cluster 2 and to a lesser extent, cluster 3 peaks were more commonly located in promoter-proximal regions (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3D.

claim: Cluster 2 and cluster 3 peaks were more commonly located in promoter-proximal regions.
source: Differences were also observed in genomic location distributions of each cluster with cluster 1 peaks showing a predominantly intergenic or intronic distribution, whereas cluster 2 and to a lesser extent, cluster 3 peaks were more commonly located in promoter-proximal regions (Figure 3D; Figure 3—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 3D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1B.

claim: ZMYM2 and TRIM28 were unable to co-precipitate under standard conditions.
source: First, we attempted to co-precipitate ZMYM2 and TRIM28 but were unable to detect co-binding under standard conditions (Figure 4A, lanes 4–6; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: ZMYM2 binding to TRIM28 was observed in the presence of NEM.
source: We therefore repeated the co-precipitation experiment in the presence of NEM (an isopeptidase inhibitor and critical to preserve protein SUMOylation) and observed ZMYM2 binding to TRIM28 (Figure 4A, lanes 1–3; Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4A.

claim: NEM addition stabilised high molecular weight SUMO conjugates and revealed the binding of ZMYM2 to SUMOylated protein(s).
source: Indeed, NEM addition stabilised high molecular weight SUMO conjugates and revealed the binding of ZMYM2 to SUMOylated protein(s) (Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1B.

claim: The SUMO binding defective ZMYM2(SIM2mut) showed weaker interactions with TRIM28 than wild-type ZMYM2.
source: Further evidence for SUMO-dependent interactions was derived from co-IP studies where the SUMO binding defective ZMYM2(SIM2mut) showed weaker interactions with TRIM28 than wild-type ZMYM2 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Interactions between ZMYM2 and TRIM28 in a cellular context were validated using PLA.
source: Interactions between ZMYM2 and TRIM28 in a cellular context were further validated using PLA (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4B.

claim: ZMYM2 and TRIM28 co-binding was validated by ChIP-qPCR.
source: These findings are consistent with the SUMO-dependent enrichment of TRIM28 occupancy on chromatin in ZMYM2 cluster 1 (Figure 2A) and this shared binding profile was validated by ChIP-qPCR (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1D.

claim: ZMYM2 depletion did not affect TRIM28 binding to a panel of its binding regions.
source: This co-binding suggests that ZMYM2 might be responsible for recruiting TRIM28 to chromatin but we found no evidence for this as ZMYM2 depletion did not affect TRIM28 binding to a panel of its binding regions (Figure 4—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1E.

claim: TRIM28 co-binds with the ZMYM2 related protein ZMYM3.
source: We also further validated our RIME experiments and examined whether interactions with the ZMYM2 paralog ZMYM3 could be verified. Co-immunoprecipitation detected co-binding of TRIM28 with the ZMYM2 related protein ZMYM3 (Figure 4—figure supplement 1F) indicating that these interactions extend to other ZMYM2 paralogs.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1F.

claim: For TRIM28, roughly equal numbers of genes were up and downregulated following depletion.
source: For TRIM28, roughly equal numbers of genes were up and downregulated, and a similar phenomenon was observed for ZMYM2 following depletion, albeit more skewed to downregulation in the case of ZMYM2 (Figure 4C; Supplementary file 4).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: There was a substantial and highly significant overlap between ZMYM2 and TRIM28 regulated genes irrespective of the directionality.
source: However, there was a substantial and highly significant overlap between ZMYM2 and TRIM28 regulated genes irrespective of the directionality (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4C with p-values.

claim: Gene regulation showing reciprocal directionality following either TRIM28 or ZMYM2 depletion showed a very small and insignificant overlap.
source: Conversely, in contrast to these similarities, gene regulation showing reciprocal directionality following either TRIM28 or ZMYM2 depletion showed a very small and insignificant overlap (Figure 4—figure supplement 1H).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Terms such as 'ossification' and 'skeletal system development' were associated with genes downregulated by both ZMYM2 and TRIM28.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis revealed different pathways associated with genes up and downregulated by both ZMYM2 and TRIM28 (Figure 4D). Terms such as 'ossification' and 'skeletal system development' were associated with the downregulated genes suggesting a disassembly of the core transcriptome associated with the cell identity (U2OS cells are derived from osteosarcomas), whereas upregulated genes contributed to more general GO terms, mainly associated with metabolism and cell responses such as 'positive regulation of phosphorylation'.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Upregulated genes following ZMYM2 and TRIM28 depletion contributed to GO terms mainly associated with metabolism and cell responses such as 'positive regulation of phosphorylation'.
source: Gene ontology (GO) analysis revealed different pathways associated with genes up and downregulated by both ZMYM2 and TRIM28 (Figure 4D). Terms such as 'ossification' and 'skeletal system development' were associated with the downregulated genes suggesting a disassembly of the core transcriptome associated with the cell identity (U2OS cells are derived from osteosarcomas), whereas upregulated genes contributed to more general GO terms, mainly associated with metabolism and cell responses such as 'positive regulation of phosphorylation'.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Very few ZMYM2 cluster 1 peaks are associated with genes commonly up- or down-regulated following ZMYM2 and TRIM28 depletion using the nearest gene model.
source: To further explore how ZMYM2 and TRIM28 work together to control gene expression, we tried to associate ZMYM2 cluster 1 peaks with genes commonly up- or down-regulated following ZMYM2 and TRIM28 depletion by using the nearest gene model. However, very few of these peaks are associated with the co-regulated genes identified from RNA-seq analysis (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Very few differentially expressed genes are found within 20 kb of a ZMYM2 peak.
source: We further investigated this possibility by comparing the number of genes deregulated following ZMYM2 depletion that are associated with ZMYM2 peaks across the entire ZMYM2 binding dataset. Very few differentially expressed genes are found within 20 kb of a ZMYM2 peak (Figure 5A), but there is an increasing association as the window size is increased.
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: The distance-dependent distribution of ZMYM2 binding regions is virtually the same as a randomly selected set of genes when considering genes that are downregulated following ZMYM2 depletion.
source: The distance-dependent distribution of ZMYM2 binding regions is virtually the same as a randomly selected set of genes when considering genes that are downregulated following ZMYM2 depletion (Figure 5A, right).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Significantly more differentially upregulated genes are associated with ZMYM2 peaks across all of the peak-gene distance brackets compared to a control set of genes.
source: However, in contrast, significantly more differentially upregulated genes are associated with ZMYM2 peaks across all of the peak-gene distance brackets compared to a control set of genes (Figure 5A, left).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5A with statistical significance indicated.

claim: ZMYM2 cluster 1 peaks show a more significant distance-based association with upregulated rather than downregulated genes.
source: Indeed when we focussed on ZMYM2 cluster 1 peaks (ie potentially ZMYM2-TRIM28 co-regulated) and the genes whose expression increased following either TRIM28 or ZMYM2 depletion (ie repressed by these factors), we found a more significant distance-based association of ZMYM2 peaks with upregulated rather than downregulated genes (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5B.

claim: TADs containing cluster 1 binding regions contained a significantly higher number of upregulated genes compared to downregulated genes compared to TADs which lacked ZMYM2 binding regions.
source: TADs containing cluster 1 binding regions contained a significantly higher number of upregulated genes compared to downregulated genes compared to TADs which lacked ZMYM2 binding regions (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5C with statistical significance indicated.

claim: A gene is more likely to be negatively regulated by ZMYM2 when located in the same TAD as a cluster 1 peak rather than being located in other TADs lacking such peaks.
source: Moreover, we also tested whether a gene is more likely to be negatively regulated by ZMYM2 when located in the same TAD as a cluster 1 peak rather than being located in other TADs lacking such peaks. The observed frequency of co-localisation was significantly higher than by chance (Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1C with statistical analysis.

claim: There is not a general spreading of transcriptional deregulation around ZMYM2 peaks in a distance-dependent manner.
source: To test this we took all of the ZMYM2 regions associated with genes upregulated by ZMYM2 depletion that resided in the same TAD and calculated the peak to TSS distance. Then we searched in the opposite direction for the TSS of genes at a similar distance (+/-25%) that resided in an adjacent TAD. We then asked whether these genes were upregulated by ZMYM2 depletion. 102 ZMYM2 peaks were positioned within these distance constraints with at least one gene in an adjacent TAD (716 genes in total). Of these genes, only 11 were upregulated following ZMYM2 depletion. There is therefore not a general spreading of transcriptional deregulation around ZMYM2 peaks in a distance-dependent manner.
evidence: This is stated in the results based on computational analysis of TAD boundaries and gene regulation.

claim: ZMYM2 peaks in all clusters were significantly closer to a TAD boundary than expected by chance.
source: We further probed the association with TAD boundaries by comparing the distances of the ZMYM2 peaks in each of the clusters to TAD boundaries with randomly selected genomic regions. In all cases, the ZMYM2 peaks were significantly closer to a TAD boundary than expected by chance (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 5D with statistical significance indicated.

claim: All three clusters of ZMYM2 binding regions showed a high degree of overlap with repetitive elements, with 80% of the regions in cluster 1 showing close proximity to these elements.
source: We therefore asked whether ZMYM2 binding regions mapped to any repetitive elements. All three clusters of ZMYM2 binding regions showed a high degree of overlap with repetitive elements, with 80% of the regions in cluster 1 showing close proximity to these elements (Figure 6A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The distribution of retrotransposon classes differed among ZMYM2 clusters, with cluster 3 and cluster 1 favouring long terminal repeats (LTRs) whereas cluster 2 regions are mainly associated with short interspersed nuclear elements (SINE).
source: However, the distribution of retrotransposon classes differed among ZMYM2 clusters, with cluster 3 and cluster 1 in particular favouring long terminal repeats (LTRs) whereas cluster 2 regions are mainly associated with short interspersed nuclear elements (SINE).
evidence: This is stated in the results based on analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: ADNP has been implicated in SINE control.
source: The latter is consistent with the higher levels of ADNP binding found in cluster 2 regions, as ADNP has been implicated in SINE control (Kaaij et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the results with citation to Kaaij et al., 2019.

claim: Cluster 3 is dominated by endogenous retrovirus (ERV)-L elements whereas cluster 1 is dominated by ERV-1 elements.
source: We further examined the distribution of subtypes of LTR elements in clusters 1 and 3 and found that cluster 3 is dominated by endogenous retrovirus (ERV)-L elements whereas cluster 1 is dominated by ERV-1 elements (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: LTRs showed upregulation following ZMYM2 loss, consistent with a repressive activity.
source: Given the association of ZMYM2 with LTRs, we next asked whether ZMYM2 represses their activity as predicted. We depleted ZMYM2 and examined the regulation of LTR expression, and found that the LTRs showed upregulation following ZMYM2 loss, consistent with a repressive activity (Figure 6D; Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6D with RT-qPCR data.

claim: Cluster 2 ZMYM2 peaks are associated with equal numbers of Alu repeats and MIR elements.
source: We also examined the distribution of subclasses of SINEs associated with cluster 2 ZMYM2 peaks and found equal numbers of Alu repeats and MIR elements (Figure 6E).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Depletion of ZMYM2 caused increased activity of several SINEs.
source: Importantly, depletion of either ZMYM2 (Figure 6F) or ADNP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) both caused increased activity of several SINEs, consistent with our designation of these retroviral elements as co-regulated by ZMYM2 and ADNP from our ChIP-seq analysis (eg Figure 6C, bottom).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6F with RT-qPCR data.

claim: Depletion of ADNP caused increased activity of several SINEs.
source: Importantly, depletion of either ZMYM2 (Figure 6F) or ADNP (Figure 6—figure supplement 1B) both caused increased activity of several SINEs, consistent with our designation of these retroviral elements as co-regulated by ZMYM2 and ADNP from our ChIP-seq analysis (eg Figure 6C, bottom).
evidence: This is stated in the results and shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1B with RT-qPCR data.

claim: ZMYM2 associates with LTR containing regions and promotes their repression in combination with the corepressor protein TRIM28.
source: Collectively, these results show that ZMYM2 associates with LTR containing regions, and promotes their repression in combination with the corepressor protein TRIM28 whereas it works alongside ADNP to control SINE element expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the combined ChIP-seq and RT-qPCR data.

claim: ZMYM2 works alongside ADNP to control SINE element expression.
source: Collectively, these results show that ZMYM2 associates with LTR containing regions, and promotes their repression in combination with the corepressor protein TRIM28 whereas it works alongside ADNP to control SINE element expression.
evidence: This is a conclusion stated in the results based on the combined ChIP-seq and RT-qPCR data.

claim: ZMYM2 has been established as an important regulator of cell fate identity and commitment, particularly at the pluripotency stage.
source: ZMYM2 has been established as an important regulator of cell fate identity and commitment, particularly at the pluripotency stage.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of established knowledge.

claim: Genetic disruptions of ZMYM2 function have been linked to disease.
source: Genetic disruptions of ZMYM2 function have been linked to disease.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a summary of established knowledge.

claim: ZMYM2 binding to TRIM28 is SUMO-dependent.
source: Interestingly, ZMYM2 binding to TRIM28 is SUMO-dependent, as retention of SUMOylation is required to detect binding by co-IP and ZMYM2 binding to cluster 1 regions require the SUMO interaction motifs in ZMYM2.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the co-IP and ChIP-seq data presented in the results.

claim: ZMYM2 is itself SUMOylated.
source: It is not currently clear what SUMO modified protein(s) are the direct binding target of ZMYM2, although ZMYM2 is itself SUMOylated (Kunapuli et al., 2006), as is TRIM28 (Lee et al., 2007), which can also act as a SUMO E3 ligase (Ivanov et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Kunapuli et al., 2006.

claim: TRIM28 is SUMOylated.
source: It is not currently clear what SUMO modified protein(s) are the direct binding target of ZMYM2, although ZMYM2 is itself SUMOylated (Kunapuli et al., 2006), as is TRIM28 (Lee et al., 2007), which can also act as a SUMO E3 ligase (Ivanov et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Lee et al., 2007.

claim: TRIM28 can act as a SUMO E3 ligase.
source: It is not currently clear what SUMO modified protein(s) are the direct binding target of ZMYM2, although ZMYM2 is itself SUMOylated (Kunapuli et al., 2006), as is TRIM28 (Lee et al., 2007), which can also act as a SUMO E3 ligase (Ivanov et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Ivanov et al., 2007.

claim: ZMYM2 was identified in reciprocal co-IP experiments with TRIM28 as a glycosylated interaction partner.
source: However, ZMYM2 was identified in reciprocal co-IP experiments with TRIM28, as a glycosylated interaction partner (Boulard et al., 2020) suggesting that multiple post-translational modifications govern the assembly and function of this complex.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Boulard et al., 2020.

claim: TRIM28 has been shown to act as a widespread repressor of retrotransposons where it is recruited by KRAB domain containing zinc finger proteins.
source: The latter observation is interesting, as TRIM28 has been shown to act as a widespread repressor of retrotransposons where it is recruited by KRAB domain containing zinc finger proteins (reviewed in Bruno et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Bruno et al., 2019.

claim: ZMYM2 is a zinc finger protein but lacks the KRAB domain but still binds to TRIM28.
source: ZMYM2 is also a zinc finger protein but lacks the KRAB domain but still binds to TRIM28, suggesting that a broader swathe of zinc finger proteins may be involved in repetitive element epigenetic repression.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the structural features of ZMYM2 and the binding data presented.

claim: TRIM28 has been shown to be able to engage directly with unmodified histone H4 tails.
source: It is also not clear what the chromatin recruitment mechanism is, although recent studies do not rule out a direct role for TRIM28 in the process as it has been shown to be able to engage directly with unmodified histone H4 tails (Bacon et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Bacon et al., 2020.

claim: ZMYM2 was identified as an important regulator of silencing of imprinting control regions which are under the control of the zinc finger protein ZFP57.
source: Indeed a recent study identified ZMYM2 as an important regulator of silencing of imprinting control regions which are under the control of the zinc finger protein ZFP57 (Butz et al., 2022).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Butz et al., 2022.

claim: ZMYM2 binding regions are generally more associated with genes that it represses rather than activates.
source: However, ZMYM2 binding regions are generally more associated with genes that it represses rather than activates, suggesting that the latter may be indirectly affected.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the distance-based association analysis presented in the results.

claim: ERV-H LTRs demarcate TADs in human pluripotent stem cells.
source: For example, the ERV-H LTRs demarcate TADs in human pluripotent stem cells (Zhang et al., 2019), and it is possible that ZMYM2-TRIM28 complexes control ERV LTR activity which in turn influence local chromatin topology.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Zhang et al., 2019.

claim: ADNP has previously been shown to play an active role in controlling chromatin domain boundary elements at SINE B2 transposable elements by blocking CTCF binding.
source: This might apply in particular to the ZMYM2-ADNP co-bound regions, as ADNP has previously been shown to play an active role in controlling chromatin domain boundary elements at SINE B2 transposable elements by blocking CTCF binding (Kaaij et al., 2019).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Kaaij et al., 2019.

claim: ZMYM2 interacts with the GTF3C complex which has previously been implicated in controlling retrotransposon transcription.
source: It is also noteworthy that ZMYM2 interacts with the GTF3C complex which has previously been implicated in controlling retrotransposon transcription (Ferrari et al., 2020).
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with citation to Ferrari et al., 2020.

claim: ZMYM2 acts directly through retrotransposon regulation, which may then potentially affect the local chromatin environment and associated coding gene expression.
source: We propose a model whereby ZMYM2 acts directly through retrotransposon regulation, which may then potentially affect the local chromatin environment and associated coding gene expression.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a proposed model based on the data presented.
